52521.e: In autumn you can hear the red deer stags roaring in the national park.
52521.m: Many red deer live in the national park.

52522.q: Are you allowed to take your dog into the national park?
52522.e: Dogs could disturb the wild animals. That is why they are not allowed in the national park, not even on a lead.
52522.m: Dogs are not allowed in the national park.

52523.q: In which village is the national park's visitor centre?
52523.e: The visitor centre in Zernez has an exhibition about the park's animals and plants.
52523.m: The national park's visitor centre is in Zernez.

52524.q: Which string instrument belongs to the folk music of the Toggenburg?
52524.e: The Toggenburg Halszither is a cittern with a long neck and metal strings. It is a typical instrument of folk music in the Toggenburg.
52524.m: The Halszither belongs to Toggenburg music.

52525.q: Which peak of the Churfirsten can you reach by cable car from the Toggenburg?
52525.e: From Unterwasser you first go to Iltios and then take the cable car up the Chäserrugg. At the top there is a wooden restaurant.
52525.m: A cable car goes up the Chäserrugg.

52526.q: How many peaks are usually counted in the Churfirsten?
52526.e: The Churfirsten are usually counted as seven peaks, though more or fewer depending on how you count. On the south side they drop steeply down to Lake Walen.
52526.m: The Churfirsten are usually counted as seven peaks.

52527.q: Which famous reformer was born in the Toggenburg in 1484?
52527.e: Ulrich Zwingli was born in the upper Toggenburg. Later he worked as a priest in Zurich.
52527.m: Ulrich Zwingli came from the Toggenburg.

52528.q: What can you do on the Sound Trail in the Toggenburg?
52528.e: Along the Sound Trail there are instruments made of wood and metal. You can play them and experience sounds.
52528.m: On the Sound Trail you can try out sounds.

52529.q: Which animal is named after the Toggenburg?
52529.e: The Toggenburg goat is a brown breed of goat with white stripes on its head.
52529.m: The Toggenburg goat is named after the valley.

52530.q: Which art is an old tradition in the Toggenburg?
52530.e: Toggenburg farmhouse painting shows cows going up to the alpine pastures, cows and farmers in bright colours.
52530.m: In the Toggenburg people paint colourful farm pictures.

52531.q: Which two villages in the upper Toggenburg are well-known holiday resorts?
52531.e: Wildhaus and Unterwasser lie in the upper Toggenburg. In winter people ski there, in summer they go hiking.
52531.m: Wildhaus and Unterwasser lie in the Toggenburg.

52532.q: Which dark bread is a speciality from Valais?
52532.e: Valais rye bread is baked from rye flour. Rye also grows in the high mountain valleys.

52533.q: What is the capital of the canton of Valais called?
52533.e: Sion is called Sitten in German. The cantonal government sits there.
52533.m: Sion is the capital of Valais.

52534.q: Why do the old wooden storehouses in Valais stand on round stone slabs?
a: So that no mice can climb in
So that they do not fall over
So that they stay warm in winter
So that they can be moved
52534.e: The old storehouses are called Stadel. Mice cannot climb over the round stone slabs, so they cannot get to the grain.
52534.m: The stone slabs under the storehouses keep mice out.

52535.q: What is special about the mountain village of Zermatt?
a: It lies on a big lake
There is never any snow there
52535.e: No normal cars drive in Zermatt. You arrive by train and get around the village in small electric vehicles.

52536.q: What is the weather often like in the Rhône valley in Valais?
52536.e: High mountains keep out many rain clouds. That is why it is often sunny and dry in the Rhône valley.
52536.m: It is often sunny and dry in Valais.

52537.q: Which cheese dish comes from Valais?
52537.e: For raclette half a wheel of cheese is melted. You eat the soft cheese with potatoes.
52537.m: Raclette is a cheese dish from Valais.

52538.q: Which orange fruit grows in especially large amounts in Valais?
52538.e: Many apricots grow in Valais. They are used to make jam, for example.

52539.q: Which train travels slowly from Zermatt to St Moritz?
52539.e: The Glacier Express takes about eight hours to travel through the Alps from Zermatt to St Moritz.
52539.m: The Glacier Express runs from Zermatt to St Moritz.

52540.q: How many stars are there on the flag of Valais?
52540.e: The 13 stars stand for the 13 old “Zenden”, or districts, of Valais.

52541.q: In which language is Switzerland called “Svizra”?
52541.e: In Romansh Switzerland is called “Svizra”. In Italian it is called “Svizzera”, in French “Suisse”.
52541.m: In Romansh Switzerland is called Svizra.

52542.q: How do you say “Good day” in Italian?
52542.e: “Buongiorno” means “Good day” in Italian. You often hear this greeting in Ticino.

52543.q: What is the biggest bilingual town in Switzerland called?
52543.e: In Biel/Bienne many people speak German and many speak French. The street signs are written in both languages.
52543.m: Biel/Bienne is the biggest bilingual town in Switzerland.

52544.q: What do people in German-speaking Switzerland mostly speak in everyday life?
52544.e: In everyday life most people in German-speaking Switzerland speak dialect, that is Swiss German. At school they also learn Standard German.
52544.m: In German-speaking Switzerland people mostly speak dialect in everyday life.

52545.q: What colours is the Swiss flag?
52545.e: The Swiss flag is red with a white cross in the middle.
52545.m: The Swiss flag is red and white.

52546.q: What can you see on the Swiss flag?
52546.e: In the middle of the red flag there is a white cross. It is a symbol of Switzerland.
52546.m: There is a white cross on the Swiss flag.

52548.q: Which symbol looks like the Swiss flag with the colours swapped?
52548.e: The symbol of the Red Cross is a red cross on a white background. It honours Switzerland by reversing its colours.
52548.m: The Red Cross symbol has the colours of the Swiss flag swapped.

52549.q: What lights up in many places in Switzerland on 1 August?
52549.e: On the national holiday bonfires burn on many hills. Children carry paper lanterns with the Swiss cross.
52549.m: Paper lanterns and bonfires light up on 1 August.

52550.q: What do many Swiss products show so that you can see they come from Switzerland?
52550.e: Many products from Switzerland carry a small Swiss cross. There are clear rules about when it may be used.
52550.m: The Swiss cross shows that something comes from Switzerland.

52551.q: Which canton is the biggest in Switzerland?
52551.e: The Grisons have the largest area of all the cantons. There are many mountains and valleys there.
52551.m: The Grisons are the biggest canton.

52552.q: In which canton do the most people live?
52552.e: The canton of Zurich has the most inhabitants. There are over 1.5 million people (as of 2024).
52552.m: The most people live in the canton of Zurich.

52554.q: Which three cantons are seen as the founders of Switzerland?
52554.e: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden formed an alliance in 1291. This is seen as the beginning of Switzerland.
52554.m: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden are the founding cantons.

52555.q: What is written before the number on Swiss number plates?
52555.e: Every Swiss number plate shows the canton's abbreviation, for example ZH for Zurich or BE for Bern.
52555.m: The canton's abbreviation is on every number plate.

52556.q: Which animal can you see on the coat of arms of Bern?
52556.e: A black bear walks across the coat of arms of Bern. The bear is the symbol of the city.
52556.m: The bear is the heraldic animal of Bern.

52557.q: Which animals can you visit in a park on the bank of the Aare in Bern?
52557.e: Bears live in the Bear Park in Bern. They used to live in the bear pit right next to it.
52557.m: Bears live in the Bear Park in Bern.

52558.q: What is the famous clock tower in Bern's old town called?
52558.e: The Zytglogge is an old tower with an astronomical clock. Shortly before every full hour, figures move on it.
52558.m: The Zytglogge is the famous clock tower of Bern.

52559.q: What are the covered walkways in Bern's old town called?
52559.e: There are many arcades in Bern's old town. Under them you can shop and stay dry even when it rains.
52559.m: In Bern's old town you walk under arcades.

52560.q: Which vegetable is the star of Bern's Zibelemärit in November?
52560.e: “Zibele” means onion. At the Zibelemärit (onion market) stallholders sell lots of onions, often plaited into strings.
52560.m: At Bern's Zibelemärit everything is about onions.

52561.q: How many members does the Federal Council, which governs in Bern, have?
52561.e: The Federal Council is the government of Switzerland. It has seven members.
52561.m: The Federal Council has seven members.

52562.q: Which neighbouring country lies to the east of Switzerland?
52562.e: To the east Switzerland borders Austria and the small country of Liechtenstein.
52562.m: Austria lies to the east of Switzerland.

52563.q: Which is Switzerland's smallest neighbouring country?
52563.e: Liechtenstein is a very small country between Switzerland and Austria. It is smaller than many cantons.

52564.q: On which big lake do Switzerland, Germany and Austria meet?
52564.e: Lake Constance lies in the north-east of Switzerland. Its shores belong to Switzerland, Germany and Austria.
52564.m: Three countries meet at Lake Constance.

52565.q: What does Switzerland not have, because it lies in the middle of Europe?
52565.e: Switzerland is a landlocked country. It has no coast, but many lakes and rivers.
52565.m: Switzerland is not by the sea.

52566.e: Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe. That is why many trains and lorries travel through Switzerland.
52566.m: Switzerland lies in the middle of Europe.

52567.q: What does Switzerland look like on the map?
52567.e: From west to east Switzerland is about 350 kilometres wide. From north to south it is only about 220 kilometres.
52567.m: Switzerland is wider than it is tall.

52568.q: Which canton forms the tip in the far south on the map?
52568.e: On the map Ticino sticks out to the south like a point. It lies south of the Alps.
52568.m: Ticino is the southern tip of Switzerland.

52569.q: Which canton lies in the far west on the map?
52569.e: Geneva lies in the far west of Switzerland. The canton is almost completely surrounded by France.
52569.m: Geneva lies in the far west of Switzerland.

52570.q: Which canton lies in the far east on the map?
52570.e: The Grisons form the easternmost part of Switzerland. There Switzerland borders Austria and Italy.
52570.m: The Grisons lie in the far east of Switzerland.

52571.q: Which big waterfall lies in the north of Switzerland near Schaffhausen?
52571.e: The Rhine Falls are one of the biggest waterfalls in Europe. They lie at Neuhausen am Rheinfall in the canton of Schaffhausen.
52571.m: The Rhine Falls are near Schaffhausen.

52572.q: Where do three countries meet in Basel?
52572.e: In Basel, Switzerland, Germany and France meet on the Rhine. This point is called the Three Countries Corner.
52572.m: Three countries meet at the Three Countries Corner in Basel.

52573.q: Which milk is Gruyère cheese made from?
52573.e: Gruyère is made from raw cow's milk. The milk comes from cows in the region.
52573.m: Gruyère is made from cow's milk.

52574.q: What does a Gruyère cheese usually look like inside?
52574.e: Gruyère has almost no holes. Its paste is firm and even.

52575.q: In German this cheese is called Greyerzer. What is it called in French?
52575.e: In French the cheese is called “Le Gruyère”. It is named after the Gruyère region (Greyerz in German).
52575.m: Greyerzer is called Gruyère in French.

52576.q: What kind of cheese is Gruyère?
52576.e: Gruyère is a hard cheese. It matures for many months and becomes firm as it does.

52577.q: What is the minimum time a Gruyère matures for?
52577.e: A Gruyère must mature in the cellar for at least about five months. Many wheels mature even longer and then taste stronger.
52577.m: A Gruyère matures for many months.

52578.q: Roughly how heavy is a whole wheel of Gruyère?
52578.e: A wheel of Gruyère usually weighs between 25 and 40 kilograms. It is round and flat.
52578.m: A wheel of Gruyère is very heavy.

52579.q: Which hot dish is Gruyère often needed for?
52579.e: Gruyère melts well. That is why it is in many recipes for cheese fondue.

52580.q: Where are the wheels of Gruyère looked after while they mature?
52580.e: The wheels lie in a damp, cool cellar. There they are regularly turned and rubbed with salt water.
52580.m: Gruyère matures in a cool cellar.

52581.q: What is the person who makes cheese from milk called?
52581.e: A cheesemaker makes cheese from milk in the cheese dairy.
52581.m: The cheesemaker turns milk into cheese.

52582.q: How can you recognise an Emmental cheese straight away?
52582.e: Emmental has big, round holes. That is why it is known all over the world.

52583.q: In which canton is the Emmental?
52583.e: The Emmental is a hilly area in the canton of Bern. The cheese gets its name from there.
52583.m: The Emmental is in the canton of Bern.

52584.q: What is the firm outer layer of a wheel of Emmental called?
52584.e: The rind is the hard outer layer of the cheese wheel. It protects the cheese inside while it matures.
52584.m: The rind protects the Emmental while it matures.

52585.q: What forms inside Emmental so that holes grow?
52585.e: Tiny bacteria in the cheese produce a gas as it matures. The gas collects and that is how the holes form.
52585.m: Gas makes the holes in Emmental.

52586.q: How heavy can a big wheel of Emmental get?
52586.e: A wheel of Emmental weighs about 75 to 120 kilograms. It is one of the biggest cheese wheels in the world.
52586.m: A wheel of Emmental is enormously heavy.

52587.q: What does Emmental usually taste like?
52587.e: Young Emmental tastes mild and slightly nutty. Older Emmental tastes stronger.

52588.q: Which milk is Emmental made from?
52588.e: Emmental is made from raw cow's milk. The cows eat grass and hay for it, but no silage.
52588.m: Emmental is made from cow's milk.

52589.q: What shape is a whole wheel of Emmental?
52589.e: A wheel of Emmental is round and flat like a big wheel. That is why people also call it a cheese wheel.
52589.m: A wheel of Emmental is round like a wheel.

52590.q: Which river is the Emmental named after?
52590.e: The Emmental is the valley of the Emme. The Emme flows through the hilly landscape and later joins the Aare.
52590.m: The Emmental is named after the River Emme.

52591.q: When are the cows up on the alpine pasture?
a: In spring, when there is still snow
52591.e: In summer fresh grass grows on the alpine pasture. That is why the cows are taken up into the mountains at this time.
52591.m: In summer the cows are on the alpine pasture.

a: A mountain pasture used in summer
52592.e: An Alp is a pasture in the mountains. Cows, cattle or goats graze there in summer.
52592.m: An Alp is a mountain pasture for the summer.

52593.q: What do cows on the alpine pasture often wear around their necks?
52593.e: The bells ring when the cows walk. That way you can hear where the animals are grazing.
52593.m: Cows on the alpine pasture often wear bells.

52594.q: What is the man called who makes cheese from the milk on the alpine pasture?
52594.e: A Senn or Sennerin (alpine dairy farmer) makes alpine cheese from fresh milk on the alpine pasture.
52594.m: The Senn makes cheese on the alpine pasture.

52595.q: What do the cows on the alpine pasture mainly eat?
52595.e: On the alpine pasture the cows eat fresh grass and lots of mountain herbs. This gives the milk a special taste.
52595.m: On the alpine pasture cows eat grass and herbs.

52596.q: What is the procession of cows up to the alpine pasture in early summer called?
a: The ascent to the alpine pasture
The descent from the alpine pasture
52596.e: In early summer the cows walk from the valley up to the alpine pasture. This is called the ascent, or “Alpaufzug”.
52596.m: During the ascent the cows go up to the alpine pasture.

52597.q: How often a day are dairy cows usually milked?
52597.e: Dairy cows are usually milked in the morning and in the evening, so twice a day.
52597.m: Dairy cows are milked twice a day.

52598.q: What do the Hérens cows in Valais do at a special festival?
52598.e: Hérens cows are strong. In the cow fights they push their heads against each other. The strongest cow becomes queen.
52598.m: Hérens cows test their strength in cow fights.

52599.e: Swiss Brown is one of the most common breeds of cow in Switzerland. The cows are brown and well suited to the mountains.
52599.m: Swiss Brown is a typical Swiss breed of cow.

52600.q: When does the descent from the alpine pasture usually take place?
52600.e: The cows stay on the alpine pasture all summer. Usually in September they return to the valley in a cheerful procession.
52600.m: The descent from the alpine pasture usually takes place in September.

52601.q: What happens during the descent from the alpine pasture?
a: The cows come down to the valley
The cows go up to the alpine pasture
52601.e: During the descent the cows return from the alpine pasture to the valley. There they spend the winter in the shed.
52601.m: During the descent the cows come back to the valley.

52602.q: What are the cows often decorated with during the descent from the alpine pasture?
52602.e: During the descent many cows wear a headdress of flowers and colourful ribbons.
52602.m: During the descent the cows wear flower decorations.

52603.q: Why do the cows leave the alpine pasture in autumn?
a: Because it gets cold up there
Because the pasture gets too small
Because there is a market in the valley
52603.e: In autumn it gets cold in the mountains and snow soon falls. Then hardly any grass grows either.
52603.m: In autumn it gets too cold on the alpine pasture.

52604.q: Which cow often wears the finest decorations during the descent from the alpine pasture?
a: The last cow in the herd
52604.e: The lead cow leads the herd. She often wears the biggest headdress and a big bell.
52604.m: The lead cow walks at the front and is beautifully decorated.

52605.q: What is the descent from the alpine pasture called in French in western Switzerland?
52605.e: In French-speaking Switzerland the descent from the alpine pasture is called “Désalpe”. Some villages hold a big festival for it.
52605.m: In French the descent from the alpine pasture is called Désalpe.

52606.q: What do the alpine herders often wear during the descent from the alpine pasture?
52606.e: During the descent the herdsmen and herdswomen often wear their beautiful traditional costume. That turns the procession into a festival.
52606.m: Many alpine herders wear traditional costume during the descent.

52607.q: What are the big, loud bells that cows wear during the descent from the alpine pasture called?
52607.e: Treicheln are big bells made of sheet metal. They make a loud, deep sound during the descent from the alpine pasture.

52608.q: Where do the cows spend the winter after the descent from the alpine pasture?
a: In the shed in the valley
On the alpine pasture in the snow
On a pasture by the lake
52608.e: After the descent the cows live at the farm in the valley. In winter they eat hay in the shed there.
52608.m: In winter the cows are in the shed in the valley.

52609.q: What colour are many SBB locomotives?
52609.e: Many SBB locomotives and trains are red. The SBB logo is red too.

52610.q: What is the French abbreviation for the SBB (Swiss Federal Railways)?
52610.e: In French the SBB is called “Chemins de fer fédéraux”, CFF for short. In Italian it is called FFS.
52610.m: In French the SBB is called CFF.

52611.q: What is the longest railway tunnel in the world, which is in Switzerland, called?
52611.e: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is about 57 kilometres long. It was opened in 2016 (the longest in the world as of 2026).
52611.m: The Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

52612.q: What is special about the Swiss railway station clock?
a: A Swiss cross in the middle
52612.e: The station clock has a red second hand with a round dot. It stops briefly at the 12.
52612.m: The station clock has a red second hand.

52613.q: Which is the biggest railway station in Switzerland?
52613.e: Huge numbers of trains arrive at and leave Zurich main station every day. It is the biggest station in Switzerland.
52613.m: Zurich main station is the biggest station in Switzerland.

52614.q: What energy do SBB trains run on?
52614.e: SBB trains run on electricity. A large part of the electricity is made with hydropower.

52615.q: What is the travel pass called that lets you use almost all trains for a whole year?
52615.e: With the general travelcard, GA for short, you can use almost all trains, buses and trams in Switzerland.
52615.m: With the GA you can travel almost everywhere in Switzerland.

52616.q: In which year was the SBB founded?
52616.e: The SBB started running in 1902. Before that, the railways belonged to different companies.

52617.q: What is the abbreviation for the Swiss franc?
52617.e: CHF is the abbreviation for the Swiss franc. CH stands for the Latin name of Switzerland.
52617.m: The abbreviation for the franc is CHF.

52618.q: Which is the smallest coin in Switzerland?
52618.e: The smallest coin is the 5-rappen piece. The 1-rappen piece has not been legal tender since 2007.
52618.m: The smallest coin is the 5-rappen piece.

52619.q: What is the big five-franc coin often called?
52619.e: In everyday speech the five-franc coin is called “Fünfliber”. It is the biggest coin in Switzerland.
52619.m: The five-franc coin is called Fünfliber.

52620.q: What colour is the ten-franc note?
52620.e: The ten-franc note is yellow. The other notes have other colours so that you can tell them apart easily.

52621.q: Which note has the highest value in Switzerland?
52621.e: The biggest banknote is the thousand-franc note. There is no five-hundred-franc note.
52621.m: The thousand-franc note is the most valuable note.

52622.q: Which neighbouring country also pays with Swiss francs?
52622.e: Liechtenstein has no currency of its own. People there also pay with Swiss francs.
52622.m: People in Liechtenstein also pay with francs.

55386.q: What is the Norwegian parliament called?
55386.e: The Norwegian parliament is called the Storting, which means something like “great assembly”. It meets in Oslo.
55386.m: The Norwegian parliament is called the Storting.

55387.q: Roughly how deep is the Sognefjord at its deepest point?
55387.e: The Sognefjord is 1308 metres deep at its deepest point. This makes it one of the deepest fjords in the world.
55387.m: The Sognefjord is over a kilometre deep.

55388.q: What is a fjord like the Lysefjord in Norway?
a: A long arm of the sea between steep mountains
A volcanic crater with a lake
A sandy desert by the sea
55388.e: Fjords were carved out by glaciers in the Ice Age and later filled by the sea. Preikestolen rises above the Lysefjord.
55388.m: Fjords are arms of the sea shaped by glaciers.

55389.q: Which organisation is Norway a member of, like Switzerland?
55389.e: Like Switzerland, Norway is not a member of the EU, but it is a member of the European Free Trade Association, EFTA. Iceland and Liechtenstein also belong to EFTA.
55389.m: Norway and Switzerland are both members of EFTA.

55390.q: Which raw materials make Norway a rich country?
55390.e: Since the 1970s Norway has extracted large amounts of oil and natural gas from the North Sea. The state invests part of the income in a huge fund.
55390.m: Oil and natural gas from the North Sea made Norway rich.

55391.q: Which group of islands in northern Norway is known for steep mountains and dried stockfish?
55391.e: The Lofoten Islands lie north of the Arctic Circle off the coast of Norway. For centuries, cod has been dried there on wooden racks to make stockfish.
55391.m: Stockfish is dried on the Lofoten Islands.

55392.q: In 1905 Norway left a union with which country?
55392.e: From 1814 to 1905, Norway and Sweden were joined in a union under one shared king. In 1905 Norway became fully independent.

55393.q: Why is a fjord often less deep at its mouth to the sea than further in?
a: There is a sill of rock and glacial debris there
Rivers deposit a lot of sand there
The tide lifts the seabed there
The fjord was filled in artificially there
55393.e: The glacier scraped the valley out deepest further inland and lost strength at its end. That is why a sill of rock and moraine debris was left behind at the mouth.
55393.m: Many fjords have a shallow sill at their mouth.

55394.q: In which country is the Göta Canal with its many locks?
55394.e: The Göta Canal was completed in 1832 and has 58 locks. Together with rivers and lakes it connects Gothenburg with the Baltic Sea.
55394.m: The Göta Canal runs right across Sweden.

55395.q: What is the second largest city in Sweden, on the west coast, called?
55395.e: Gothenburg lies on the Kattegat and has the largest port in Scandinavia. Malmö is the third largest city in Sweden.
55395.m: Gothenburg is the second largest city in Sweden.

55396.q: What is Vättern, a large lake in Sweden, especially known for?
55396.e: Vättern is in southern Sweden and is the country’s second largest lake. Its water is so clean that you could drink it almost anywhere.
55396.m: Vättern is a large lake with very clear water.

55397.q: In which city does the Riksdag, the Swedish parliament, meet?
55397.e: The Riksdag is the Swedish parliament with 349 seats. It meets in the capital, Stockholm.
55397.m: The Swedish parliament, the Riksdag, meets in Stockholm.

55398.q: What are the many small rocky islands off the coast of Stockholm called?
55398.e: Off Stockholm there are about 30,000 islands and rocks, the Stockholm archipelago. The skerries were worn smooth by glaciers.
55398.m: There are thousands of skerries off Stockholm.

55399.q: After France and Spain, which country is the largest in the EU by area?
55399.e: Sweden covers about 450,000 square kilometres. This puts it in third place in the EU, just ahead of Germany with about 357,000 square kilometres.
55399.m: Sweden is the third largest country in the EU.

55400.q: In which year did Sweden and Finland join the European Union?
55400.e: Sweden, Finland and Austria became members of the EU on 1 January 1995. Norway rejected joining in a referendum.
55400.m: Sweden and Finland have been in the EU since 1995.

55401.q: What is the Stockholm underground especially known for?
55401.e: Over 90 of its roughly 100 stations are decorated with paintings, sculptures or mosaics. That is why the Tunnelbana is called the longest art gallery in the world.
55401.m: The Stockholm underground is full of art.

55402.q: In which year did Sweden join NATO?
55402.e: Sweden became a member of NATO in March 2024. Before that it had stayed out of military alliances for over 200 years.
55402.m: Sweden has been in NATO since 2024.

55403.q: What do the Finns call their country in their own language?
55403.e: In Finnish, Finland is called Suomi. That is why euro coins and stamps often say “Suomi Finland”.
55403.m: Finland is called Suomi in Finnish.

55404.q: Which language is Finnish closely related to?
55404.e: Finnish is not an Indo-European language but belongs to the Uralic language family. It is most closely related to Estonian, and distantly also to Hungarian.
55404.m: Finnish and Estonian are closely related languages.

55405.q: Which group of islands between Finland and Sweden belongs to Finland but speaks Swedish?
55405.e: The Åland Islands are an autonomous region of Finland with over 6700 islands and skerries. The only official language there is Swedish.
55405.m: Swedish is spoken on the Åland Islands, even though they belong to Finland.

55406.q: From which country did Finland become independent in 1917?
55406.e: From 1809 Finland was a Grand Duchy under the Russian tsar. On 6 December 1917 it declared its independence.
55406.m: Finland became independent from Russia in 1917.

55407.q: Which realm did Finland belong to when Helsinki was founded in 1550?
55407.e: The Swedish king Gustav I Vasa founded Helsinki in 1550 as a trading town. At that time Finland had already belonged to Sweden for centuries.
55407.m: Helsinki was founded by a Swedish king.

55408.q: Which city was the capital of Finland before Helsinki?
55408.e: Turku is the oldest city in Finland and was the centre of the country for a long time. In 1812 the capital was moved to Helsinki.
55408.m: Turku used to be the capital of Finland.

55409.q: In which year did Finland become a member of NATO?
55409.e: Finland joined NATO in April 2023. Before that the country stayed out of military alliances for a long time.
55409.m: Finland has been a member of NATO since 2023.

55410.q: What is the Kalevala from Finland?
a: A collection of old heroic songs
55410.e: The Kalevala was put together from old folk songs by Elias Lönnrot in the 19th century. It is Finland’s national epic.
55410.m: The Kalevala is Finland’s national epic.

55411.q: In which city does the Danish parliament meet?
55411.e: The Danish parliament meets in Christiansborg Palace in the capital, Copenhagen.
55411.m: The Danish parliament sits in Copenhagen.

55412.q: The Danish parliament is called the Folketing. What does this name mean?
55412.e: “Folk” means people and “ting” means assembly. The Folketing also includes two members each from Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
55412.m: The Danish parliament is called the Folketing.

55413.q: Roughly how high is the highest natural point in Denmark?
55413.e: Denmark’s highest point, Møllehøj in Jutland, is only about 171 metres high. Denmark is one of the flattest countries in Europe.
55413.m: Denmark has no hill higher than 200 metres.

55414.q: Which Danish island lies far to the east in the middle of the Baltic Sea?
55414.e: Bornholm lies between Sweden and Poland, about 150 kilometres east of Copenhagen. The island is known for its round churches.
55414.m: Bornholm is a Danish island far to the east.

55415.q: What does the Danish name København mean in English?
55415.e: Even in the Middle Ages, Copenhagen was an important trading place on the Øresund. That is why the name means “merchants’ harbour”.

55416.q: From which energy source does a very large share of Denmark’s electricity come?
55416.e: Denmark has many wind farms on land and at sea. For some years now, about half of its electricity has come from wind power.
55416.m: Denmark produces a lot of electricity with wind power.

55417.q: In which country do long bridges such as the Great Belt link lead from island to island?
55417.e: Denmark is made up of many islands. The Great Belt link crosses the Great Belt from Zealand to Funen.
55417.m: The Great Belt link is in Denmark.

55418.q: Which famous play by Shakespeare is set in Denmark?
55418.e: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark. The play is set in Kronborg Castle north of Copenhagen.
55418.m: Shakespeare’s Hamlet is set in Denmark.

55419.q: Roughly how much bigger than Switzerland is Iceland?
a: About two and a half times
55419.e: Iceland covers about 103,000 square kilometres, Switzerland about 41,000. 103,000 divided by 41,000 is about 2.5.
55419.m: Iceland is about two and a half times the size of Switzerland.

55420.q: In which Icelandic national park can you walk in a rift between two tectonic plates?
55420.e: In Þingvellir National Park you can clearly see how the North American and the Eurasian plates are drifting apart. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
55420.m: In Þingvellir you can see the edge of two tectonic plates.

55421.q: What does the name Reykjavík mean in English?
55421.e: The first settlers saw steam rising from hot springs and thought it was smoke. So they named the place “smoky bay”.

55422.q: In which capital city is Hallgrímskirkja, whose shape is reminiscent of basalt columns?
55422.e: Hallgrímskirkja is about 75 metres high and one of the tallest buildings in Iceland. It is the landmark of Reykjavík.
55422.m: Hallgrímskirkja is the landmark of Reykjavík.

55423.q: What does the ending “-dóttir” in many Icelandic surnames mean?
55423.e: In Iceland most people form their surname from their father’s first name. A daughter of Jón, for example, is called Jónsdóttir, a son Jónsson.
55423.m: Icelandic surnames say whose child you are.

55424.q: Which island south of Iceland was formed from 1963 onwards by a volcanic eruption in the sea?
55424.e: Surtsey grew out of the sea during an eruption from 1963 to 1967. Researchers there watch how plants and animals settle on new land.
55424.m: Surtsey is a young volcanic island.

55425.q: What is the Althing in Iceland?
55425.e: The Althing is the parliament of Iceland. It was founded in 930 and is considered one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
55425.m: Iceland’s parliament is called the Althing.

55426.q: What does Iceland not have, even though it is a NATO member?
55426.e: Iceland is a founding member of NATO, but it has no armed forces of its own. The Icelandic Coast Guard looks after safety at sea.
55426.m: Iceland has no army of its own.

55427.q: Where does almost all of Iceland’s electricity come from?
55427.e: Iceland uses its many rivers and the heat from inside the Earth. Most houses are also heated with geothermal energy.
55427.m: Iceland gets its electricity from hydropower and geothermal energy.

55428.q: Norway’s highest mountains are in Jotunheimen. What does this name mean?
55428.e: In old Norse legends the Jotuns are giants. In Jotunheimen there are over 250 peaks higher than 1900 metres.
55428.m: Jotunheimen means home of the giants.

55429.q: Which animal with long, thick fur lives in the wild in Norway’s Dovrefjell mountains?
55429.e: Musk oxen were brought from Greenland to the Dovrefjell in the 20th century. Their fur protects them from icy cold.
55429.m: Musk oxen live in the Dovrefjell.

55430.q: What else are the Scandinavian Mountains called?
55430.e: The Scandinavian Mountains are also called the Scandes. They stretch for about 1700 kilometres through Norway and Sweden.
55430.m: The Scandinavian Mountains are also called the Scandes.

55431.q: What is the treeless upland above the tree line called in Norway?
55431.e: A fjell is a wide, bare upland above the tree line. It is typical of the Scandinavian Mountains.
55431.m: A fjell is a treeless upland in Scandinavia.

55432.q: How old are the Scandinavian Mountains compared with the Alps?
a: Only formed after the Ice Age
55432.e: The Scandinavian Mountains formed about 400 million years ago and have been worn down a great deal since then. The Alps are much younger and therefore higher and more rugged.
55432.m: The Scandinavian Mountains are much older than the Alps.

55433.q: What is the steep Norwegian mountain road with eleven hairpin bends called?
55433.e: Trollstigen winds up a steep rock face in eleven tight bends. In winter the road is closed because of snow.
55433.m: Trollstigen is a winding mountain road in Norway.

55434.q: Which wild animals live in large herds on the Hardangervidda in Norway?
55434.e: The Hardangervidda is considered the largest plateau in Europe. The largest herds of wild reindeer in Europe live there.
55434.m: Wild reindeer live on the Hardangervidda.

55435.q: Which side of the Scandinavian Mountains gets the most rain?
a: The western side facing the Atlantic
The eastern side facing the Baltic Sea
55435.e: Moist air from the Atlantic rises on the western side, cools down and falls as rain. That is why Bergen is one of the rainiest cities in Europe.
55435.m: It rains most on the western side of the mountains.

55436.q: Which animals do many Sami traditionally breed?
55436.e: The Sami live in the far north of Europe. Reindeer herding is an important part of their culture.

a: In the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia
55437.e: The Sami are a people of the far north of Europe. They call their area Sápmi, often called Lapland in English.
55437.m: The Sami live in the north of Europe.

55438.q: What do the Sami call the area where they live in their own language?
55438.e: Sápmi covers the north of Norway, Sweden and Finland as well as the Russian Kola Peninsula. In English it is often called Lapland.
55438.m: The land of the Sami is called Sápmi.

55439.q: Across how many countries is the area where the Sami live spread?
55439.e: The Sami live in Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia. That makes four countries.
55439.m: The Sami area stretches across four countries.

55440.q: Which Finnish town lies on the Arctic Circle and is seen as the home of Father Christmas?
55440.e: Rovaniemi is the capital of Finnish Lapland. The well-known Santa Claus Village lies there on the Arctic Circle.
55440.m: Rovaniemi lies on the Arctic Circle in Finland.

55441.q: Which animals did the Sami herd when they lived in tents called lavvu?
55441.e: The Sami in northern Europe moved around with their reindeer herds. A lavvu could be put up and taken down quickly.

55442.q: What are the elected assemblies of the Sami in Norway, Sweden and Finland called?
55442.e: In all three countries the Sami elect their own parliament, the Sami Parliament. It deals with Sami language, culture and reindeer herding.
55442.m: The Sami have their own parliament.

55443.q: Which raw material is mined near the town of Kiruna in northern Sweden?
55443.e: Beneath Kiruna lies one of the largest iron ore mines in the world. Because the ground is sinking, the town is being rebuilt further east.
55443.m: Iron ore is mined in Kiruna.

55444.q: What is the traditional singing of the Sami called?
55444.e: A joik is a song that sings about a person, an animal or a landscape. It is one of the oldest musical traditions in Europe.
55444.m: The traditional song of the Sami is called a joik.

55445.q: When did the Baltic Sea take on its present form?
a: In the time of the dinosaurs
55445.e: After the glaciers melted about 10,000 years ago, the basin filled with meltwater and seawater. This makes the Baltic Sea a very young sea.
55445.m: The Baltic Sea formed after the last Ice Age.

55446.q: What is the largest island in the Baltic Sea called?
55446.e: Gotland belongs to Sweden and covers about 3000 square kilometres. Its capital, Visby, has a medieval town wall.
55446.m: Gotland is the largest island in the Baltic Sea.

55447.q: What is the northern part of the Baltic Sea between Sweden and Finland, which often freezes in winter, called?
55447.e: The Gulf of Bothnia has very little salt and lies far to the north. That is why it is often covered with ice in winter.
55447.m: The Gulf of Bothnia lies between Sweden and Finland.

55448.q: On which part of the Baltic Sea are Helsinki, Tallinn and St Petersburg?
55448.e: The Gulf of Finland reaches far east to St Petersburg. Helsinki is on its northern coast, Tallinn on its southern coast.
55448.m: Helsinki and Tallinn are on the Gulf of Finland.

55449.q: How many countries border the Baltic Sea?
55449.e: The countries on its shores are Germany, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Russia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. That makes nine countries.
55449.m: Nine countries border the Baltic Sea.

55450.q: Which is the largest city on the Baltic coast?
55450.e: St Petersburg has over five million inhabitants and lies at the mouth of the Neva. No other Baltic city is as big.
55450.m: St Petersburg is the largest city on the Baltic Sea.

55451.q: Roughly how deep is the Baltic Sea on average?
55451.e: On average the Baltic Sea is only about 52 metres deep. The deepest point, the Landsort Deep off Sweden, is about 460 metres.
55451.m: The Baltic Sea is a shallow sea.

55452.q: Which medieval league of towns controlled trade on the Baltic Sea for a long time?
55452.e: The Hanseatic League was an alliance of merchants and towns such as Lübeck, Gdańsk and Visby. It traded in fish, salt, grain and furs.
55452.m: The Hanseatic League shaped trade on the Baltic Sea.

55453.q: In which country is the North Cape?
55453.e: The North Cape is in the very north of Norway on the island of Magerøya. A tunnel under the sea connects the island with the mainland.
55453.m: The North Cape is in Norway.

55454.q: What can visitors to the North Cape experience in summer?
55454.e: In summer the sun does not set at the North Cape for weeks. You can even see it in the sky at midnight.
55454.m: The midnight sun shines at the North Cape in summer.

55455.q: Which well-known cape in the north of Norway is often seen as the northernmost point of Europe?
55455.e: The North Cape is a famous rock high above the sea. Strictly speaking it is on an island; the northernmost point of the mainland is Kinnarodden.
55455.m: The North Cape is in the far north of Europe.

55456.q: Roughly how high is the cliff of the North Cape?
55456.e: The North Cape is a rock plateau that rises steeply about 307 metres out of the sea. From the top you look out over the Arctic Ocean.
55456.m: The cliff of the North Cape is about 300 metres high.

55457.q: Which well-known monument stands on the plateau of the North Cape?
a: A model of the Eiffel Tower
55457.e: The steel globe is the landmark of the North Cape. Almost every visitor takes a photo there.
55457.m: There is a steel globe on the North Cape.

55458.q: Who gave the North Cape its name in 1553?
55458.e: The English seafarer Richard Chancellor sailed past it in 1553 while searching for a sea route to Asia. He named the rock “North Cape”.
55458.m: An English seafarer named the North Cape.

55459.q: Where is the North Cape in relation to the Arctic Circle?
55459.e: The North Cape lies at about 71 degrees north, the Arctic Circle at about 66.5 degrees north. So the North Cape lies clearly further north.
55459.m: The North Cape lies north of the Arctic Circle.

55460.q: Which sea lies east of the North Cape?
55460.e: At the North Cape the Norwegian Sea meets the Barents Sea. The Barents Sea reaches as far as the Russian coast.
55460.m: The Barents Sea begins east of the North Cape.

55462.q: Roughly how many people live on the Faroe Islands (as of 2025)?
55462.e: About 55,000 people live on the Faroe Islands. That is about as many as in the town of Biel/Bienne.
55462.m: Only a few tens of thousands of people live on the Faroe Islands.

55463.q: Which country do the Faroe Islands belong to?
55463.e: The Faroe Islands lie in the North Atlantic between Iceland and Norway. They belong to Denmark but largely govern themselves.
55463.m: The Faroe Islands belong to Denmark.

55464.q: What is special about the Eysturoy Tunnel on the Faroe Islands?
a: A railway station under the sea
55464.e: The Eysturoy Tunnel was opened in 2020 and connects three places. Its branches meet in a roundabout under the seabed.
55464.m: There is a roundabout under the sea in the Faroe Islands.

55465.q: What is special about the Faroe Islands with regard to the EU?
a: They are not part of the EU
They are an EU country of their own
55465.e: Denmark is a member of the EU, but the Faroe Islands decided against joining. This lets them manage their fishing themselves.
55465.m: The Faroe Islands are not part of the EU, even though Denmark is a member.

55466.q: What is almost completely missing from the landscape of the Faroe Islands?
55466.e: Because of the strong wind, the cool climate and the many sheep, hardly any trees grow on the Faroe Islands. The islands are covered with grass and moss.
55466.m: There are hardly any trees on the Faroe Islands.

55467.q: Which language is spoken in everyday life on the Faroe Islands?
55467.e: Faroese is a North Germanic language related to Icelandic. At school the children also learn Danish.
55467.m: Faroese is spoken on the Faroe Islands.

55468.q: Which branch of the economy is the most important for the Faroe Islands?
55468.e: Fish and fish products, including from salmon farming, make up most of the exports. The sea is the most important source of livelihood for the Faroe Islands.
55468.m: Fishing is the most important industry for the Faroe Islands.

55469.q: Roughly how many lakes are there in Finland?
55469.e: Finland is called the “land of a thousand lakes”, but it has far more. About 188,000 lakes larger than 500 square metres are counted.
55469.m: Finland has far more than a thousand lakes.

55470.q: What is the largest lake in Finland called?
55470.e: Saimaa is in south-eastern Finland and is made up of many connected lake basins with thousands of islands. It is the largest lake in the country.
55470.m: Saimaa is the largest lake in Finland.

55471.q: Which rare animal lives only in Finland’s Lake Saimaa?
55471.e: The Saimaa ringed seal is a seal that lives only in the fresh water of this lake. It is highly endangered and strictly protected.
55471.m: A rare freshwater seal lives in Saimaa.

55472.q: How were most of Finland’s lakes formed?
55472.e: Ice Age glaciers ground hollows into the rock and left debris behind. After the ice melted, the hollows filled with water.
55472.m: Finland’s lakes were formed by the Ice Age.

55473.q: What covers about three quarters of Finland’s area?
55473.e: Finland is one of the most forested countries in Europe. That is why wood and paper are important exports.
55473.m: Most of Finland is covered with forest.

55474.q: What is the largest lake in Europe called?
55474.e: Lake Ladoga is in Russia near St Petersburg. It is much bigger than any lake in central Europe.
55474.m: Lake Ladoga is the largest lake in Europe.

55475.q: In which country is the large lake Päijänne?
55475.e: Päijänne is the second largest lake in Finland. A long rock tunnel carries its water to Helsinki as drinking water.
55475.m: Päijänne is a large lake in Finland.

55476.q: What shaped Finland’s landscape with its many lakes and long gravel ridges?
55476.e: In the Ice Age Finland lay under thick ice. Glaciers dug out lake basins, and meltwater left behind long gravel ridges called eskers.
55476.m: Ice Age glaciers shaped Finland’s lakes.

55478.q: Which two countries does the Øresund Bridge connect?
55478.e: The Øresund link was opened in 2000. Before that, only ferries ran between Denmark and Sweden here.
55478.m: The Øresund Bridge connects Denmark and Sweden.

55479.q: Roughly how long is the Øresund Bridge itself?
55479.e: The bridge itself is about 7.8 kilometres long. Together with an island and a tunnel, the whole link is about 16 kilometres long.
55479.m: The Øresund Bridge is about 8 kilometres long.

55480.q: Which two countries does the Øresund link with its bridge and tunnel connect?
55480.e: The Øresund link runs from Copenhagen to Malmö. On the artificial island of Peberholm the route changes from tunnel to bridge.
55480.m: The Øresund link connects Denmark and Sweden.

55481.q: Why does part of the Øresund link run through a tunnel?
a: Because of the airport and shipping
55481.e: Tall bridge towers would have disturbed nearby Copenhagen Airport. Also, large ships needed to be able to sail freely through the Øresund.
55481.m: The tunnel protects air traffic and shipping.

55482.q: How is the Øresund Bridge built?
a: Railway on top, cycle path below
55482.e: The bridge has two levels. Cars drive on the upper deck and trains run on the lower deck.
55482.m: On the Øresund Bridge, cars go on top and trains below.

55483.q: Which two cities does the Øresund link connect?
55483.e: The link runs from Copenhagen on the island of Zealand to Malmö in southern Sweden.
55483.m: The Øresund Bridge connects Copenhagen and Malmö.

55484.q: What type of bridge is the main part of the Øresund Bridge?
55484.e: In the main part, steel cables stretched at an angle from tall pylons to the roadway carry the bridge. The pylons are about 200 metres high.
55484.m: The Øresund Bridge is a cable-stayed bridge.

55485.q: Which four parts together make up the United Kingdom?
55485.e: Three parts are on the large island, one is in the north-east of the island of Ireland. The Republic of Ireland is a separate country.
55485.m: The United Kingdom has four parts.

55486.q: What is the difference between “Great Britain” and the “United Kingdom”?
a: Only the United Kingdom includes Northern Ireland
Only the United Kingdom includes Wales
55486.e: Great Britain is the large island with England, Scotland and Wales. The United Kingdom also includes Northern Ireland.
55486.m: The United Kingdom is Great Britain plus Northern Ireland.

55487.q: What is the flag of the United Kingdom called?
55487.e: The flag is called the Union Jack or Union Flag. It combines the crosses of the patron saints of England, Scotland and Ireland.
55487.m: The Union Jack combines the crosses of several parts of the country.

55488.q: Which cross in the flag of the United Kingdom stands for Scotland?
a: The white cross of St Andrew
The red cross of St George
The red cross of St Patrick
The yellow cross of St David
55488.e: Scotland’s flag shows a white diagonal St Andrew’s cross on a blue background. It forms the background of the Union Jack.
55488.m: Scotland’s symbol is the diagonal St Andrew’s cross.

55489.q: What form of government does the United Kingdom have?
55489.e: The head of state is a king or queen, but the country is governed by Parliament and the Prime Minister. Charles III has been king since 2022.
55489.m: In the United Kingdom, Parliament governs under the Crown.

55490.q: Which is the largest island of the British Isles?
55490.e: Great Britain is the largest island of the British Isles and the largest island in Europe. Ireland is the second largest.
55490.m: Great Britain is the largest island in Europe.

55491.q: Roughly how many people live in the United Kingdom (as of 2024)?
55491.e: In mid-2024 about 69 million people lived in the United Kingdom. That is almost eight times as many as in Switzerland.
55491.m: Almost eight times as many people live in the United Kingdom as in Switzerland.

55492.q: Which people founded the settlement that grew into London?
55492.e: The Romans founded the settlement of Londinium around the year AD 50. Today's capital grew out of it.

55493.q: What is special about the London Underground, the “Tube”?
a: It is the oldest underground railway in the world
It runs under the sea to France
55493.e: The London Underground opened in 1863. It is the oldest underground railway in the world.
55493.m: The London Tube is the oldest underground railway in the world.

55494.q: What is kept in the Tower of London?
55494.e: The British Crown Jewels are displayed in the Tower of London, an old fortress on the Thames. It was once also used as a prison.
55494.m: The Crown Jewels are kept in the Tower of London.

55495.q: Which part of London is famous for the Prime Meridian?
55495.e: The Prime Meridian runs through the observatory in Greenwich. Lines of longitude and world time are counted from there.
55495.m: The counting of longitude starts in Greenwich.

55496.q: What is the name of London's largest airport?
55496.e: Heathrow in west London is the largest airport in the United Kingdom. It is one of the busiest airports in the world.

55497.q: Which big city lies on the Thames?
55497.e: The Thames rises in the west of England and flows east right through London to the North Sea.

55498.q: Which two universities hold a famous rowing race on the Thames every year?
55498.e: In the Boat Race, eights from Oxford and Cambridge row against each other on the Thames in London. The race has been held since 1829.
55498.m: Oxford and Cambridge row against each other in the Boat Race.

55499.q: Which London bridge over the Thames can be raised in the middle?
55499.e: Tower Bridge has two towers and a bascule bridge that opens for large ships. It opened in 1894.
55499.m: Tower Bridge can open for ships.

55500.q: What is the name for the mouth of the Thames, which gets wider and wider?
55500.e: The Thames flows into the sea through an estuary, a funnel-shaped river mouth. There, river water mixes with seawater because of the tides.
55500.m: A funnel-shaped river mouth is called an estuary.

55501.q: Which part of the United Kingdom has the most inhabitants?
55501.e: Over 80 per cent of the population of the United Kingdom live in England. It is also the largest part by area.
55501.m: England is the largest part of the United Kingdom.

55502.q: Which cross is shown on the flag of England?
a: A red cross on a white background
A white cross on a red background
A white cross on a blue background
A yellow cross on a green background
55502.e: The flag of England is the Cross of St George: a red cross on a white background. The Swiss flag has exactly the opposite colours.
55502.m: England's flag is a red cross on white.

55503.q: Which is the largest city in Scotland?
55503.e: Glasgow lies on the River Clyde in the west of Scotland. About a third of Scotland's population live in the Greater Glasgow area.

55504.q: What is the capital of Northern Ireland?
55504.e: Belfast is the capital and largest city of Northern Ireland. It lies at the mouth of the River Lagan.
55504.m: Belfast is the capital of Northern Ireland.

55505.q: Which famous ship was built in Belfast?
55505.e: The Titanic was built at the Harland and Wolff shipyard in Belfast. It sank on its first voyage in 1912.
55505.m: The Titanic came from a shipyard in Belfast.

55506.q: What is the name of the coast in Northern Ireland with thousands of six-sided basalt columns?
55506.e: The Giant's Causeway is made up of about 40,000 basalt columns. They formed when lava cooled slowly.
55506.m: The Giant's Causeway was formed from cooled lava.

55507.q: Which country does Northern Ireland belong to?
55507.e: Like England, Scotland and Wales, Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom. The rest of the island forms the country of Ireland.
55507.m: Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.

55508.q: Which city is known as the “capital of the Highlands”?
55508.e: Inverness lies at the northern end of the Great Glen by the Moray Firth. It is the administrative and shopping centre of the Highlands.
55508.m: Inverness is the capital of the Highlands.

55509.q: How do the Highlands differ from the Lowlands in Scotland?
a: The Highlands are mountainous and thinly populated
The Highlands are flat and densely populated
The Highlands are on an island
55509.e: The Highlands in the north are rugged, mountainous and thinly populated. The big cities such as Glasgow and Edinburgh lie in the flatter Lowlands in the south.
55509.m: The Highlands are Scotland's mountainous uplands.

55510.q: Which famous loch lies in the long valley of the Great Glen in the Scottish Highlands?
55510.e: The Great Glen runs right across Scotland. It contains several lochs, the best known being Loch Ness with its legendary monster.
55510.m: Loch Ness lies in the Great Glen.

55511.q: Which canal runs through the Great Glen, linking the east and west coasts of Scotland?
55511.e: The Caledonian Canal links several lochs in the Great Glen, including Loch Ness. It was built in the 19th century.
55511.m: The Caledonian Canal runs right across the Highlands.

55512.e: A clan is a large family group sharing a name, for example MacDonald. Each clan has its own checked tartan pattern.
55512.m: A Scottish clan is a large family sharing a name.

55513.q: Which large wild animals live in the Scottish Highlands?
55513.e: Many red deer live in the Highlands. In the Cairngorms National Park, the largest national park in Britain, there are even reindeer.
55513.m: Many red deer live in the Highlands.

55514.q: Which Swiss peak is about 1150 metres higher than Ben Nevis at 1345 metres?
55514.e: 2502 minus 1345 is 1157 metres. So the Säntis is about 1150 metres higher than the highest mountain in Britain.
55514.m: The Säntis is more than 1000 metres higher than Ben Nevis.

55515.q: In which part of the United Kingdom is Ben Nevis?
55515.e: Ben Nevis lies in the Scottish Highlands on the west coast of Scotland.

55516.q: Why is there often snow or fog on the summit of Ben Nevis, even in summer?
a: Because of the damp, cool maritime climate
Because it is at the North Pole
Because it is over 4000 metres high
55516.e: Westerly winds bring a lot of damp air from the Atlantic to the mountain. So the summit is usually in cloud, and snow lasts a long time.
55516.m: The maritime climate often makes Ben Nevis foggy and wet.

55517.q: What stood on the summit of Ben Nevis from 1883 to 1904?
55517.e: A weather observatory was run on the summit from 1883 to 1904. Its ruins can still be seen today.
55517.m: The weather used to be measured on Ben Nevis.

55518.q: What is Ben Nevis known for?
a: It is the highest mountain in Britain
It is the highest mountain in Europe
It is on an island in the Atlantic
55518.e: At 1345 metres, Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Britain. By Swiss standards it is rather small.
55518.m: Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in Britain.

55519.q: Which type of rock makes up a large part of Ben Nevis?
55519.e: Ben Nevis is the remains of an ancient volcano that collapsed about 350 million years ago. Ice Age glaciers later shaped it.
55519.m: Ben Nevis is the remains of an ancient volcano.

55520.q: What does Edinburgh Castle stand on?
55520.e: The castle stands on Castle Rock, the remains of an extinct volcano. From there it looks out over the whole Old Town.
55520.m: Edinburgh Castle sits on an old volcanic rock.

55521.q: What is the name of the main street of Edinburgh's Old Town between the castle and the palace?
55521.e: The Royal Mile runs from Edinburgh Castle down to Holyrood Palace. It is about one Scottish mile long.
55521.m: The Royal Mile links the castle and the palace in Edinburgh.

55522.q: Which big cultural festival takes place in Edinburgh every August?
55522.e: The Edinburgh International Festival and the Fringe take place in August. The Fringe is said to be the largest arts festival in the world.
55522.m: In August, Edinburgh becomes a festival city.

55523.q: What is the name of the hill in the middle of Edinburgh that is an old volcano?
55523.e: Arthur's Seat is 251 metres high and lies in Holyrood Park. You can climb it right in the middle of the city.
55523.m: Arthur's Seat is a volcanic hill in Edinburgh.

55524.q: Edinburgh is the capital of which part of the United Kingdom?
55524.e: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland. But Scotland's largest city is Glasgow.
55524.m: Edinburgh is the capital of Scotland.

55525.q: Where does the Scottish Parliament meet in Edinburgh?
55525.e: The Scottish Parliament has its building in the Holyrood area. It has existed in this form since 1999.
55525.m: Holyrood is the seat of the Scottish Parliament.

55526.q: Which well-known children's author wrote parts of her wizard novels in cafés in Edinburgh?
55526.e: J. K. Rowling lived in Edinburgh and worked on the Harry Potter books there. Some places in the city are said to have inspired her.
55526.m: Harry Potter was partly written in Edinburgh.

55527.q: Which is the longest river in Ireland and the British Isles?
55527.e: The Shannon is about 360 kilometres long and flows through Ireland from north to south. It is a little longer than the Thames.
55527.m: The Shannon is the longest river in the British Isles.

55528.q: Who was the first person to cross the English Channel by aeroplane in 1909?
55528.e: The Frenchman Louis Blériot flew from Calais to Dover on 25 July 1909. The flight took about 37 minutes.
55528.m: Louis Blériot was the first to fly across the English Channel in 1909.

55529.q: Which group of islands in the English Channel lies close to France but belongs to the British Crown?
55529.e: The Channel Islands, including Jersey and Guernsey, lie off the coast of Normandy. They are not part of the United Kingdom, but belong to the British Crown.
55529.m: Jersey and Guernsey are Channel Islands of the British Crown.

55530.q: Under which sea does the Channel Tunnel run?
55530.e: The Channel Tunnel runs under the English Channel from Folkestone in England to Coquelles near Calais in France.
55530.m: The Channel Tunnel lies under the English Channel.

55531.q: Off which coast of Scotland are the Hebrides?
55531.e: The Hebrides lie in the Atlantic off the west coast of Scotland. There are the Inner and the Outer Hebrides.
55531.m: The Hebrides lie off Scotland's west coast.

55532.q: Which well-known island of the Inner Hebrides is linked to the mainland by a bridge?
55532.e: The Isle of Skye has been reachable by the Skye Bridge since 1995. It is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides.
55532.m: Skye is the largest island of the Inner Hebrides.

55533.q: Which language is still spoken by many people in the Outer Hebrides?
55533.e: Scottish Gaelic is more widespread in the Outer Hebrides than anywhere else in Scotland. Place signs are often in two languages.
55533.m: The Gaelic language lives on in the Outer Hebrides.

55534.q: What is Harris Tweed from the Outer Hebrides?
55534.e: Harris Tweed is woven by hand at home in the Outer Hebrides. Only cloth woven this way may carry the name.
55534.m: Harris Tweed is a woollen cloth from the Hebrides.

55535.q: Who mainly lives on the abandoned islands of St Kilda today?
55535.e: The islands of St Kilda lie far out in the Atlantic. In 1930 the last inhabitants were taken to the mainland; today huge colonies of seabirds nest there.
55535.m: Today St Kilda is home mainly to seabirds.

a: Off the north coast of Scotland
Off the south coast of England
Off the west coast of Ireland
55536.e: The Orkney Islands lie north of the Scottish mainland between the Atlantic and the North Sea. Further north still are the Shetland Islands.
55536.m: Orkney lies north of the Scottish mainland.

55537.q: What did a storm uncover on the Orkney Islands in 1850?
a: A Roman town made of marble
A Viking ship made of gold
55537.e: The Stone Age village of Skara Brae is about 5000 years old. You can still see beds and shelves made of stone there.
55537.m: There is a Stone Age village on Orkney.

55538.q: Which country did the Orkney Islands belong to until the 15th century?
55538.e: The Orkney Islands were in Norse hands for a long time and only passed to Scotland as a pledge in 1468. That is why many place names are of Norse origin.
55538.m: The Orkney Islands used to be Norwegian.

55539.q: Which country do the Orkney Islands belong to today?
55539.e: The Orkney Islands lie north of the Scottish mainland and belong to Scotland. The main town is Kirkwall.
55539.m: The Orkney Islands belong to Scotland.

55540.q: In which part of the UK is the Lake District?
55540.e: The Lake District is in the north-west of England in the county of Cumbria. It is a national park with many lakes and mountains.
55540.m: The Lake District is in the north-west of England.

55541.q: What is the Lake District especially good for?
55541.e: The Lake District is a national park with many lakes and mountains. Scafell Pike, the highest mountain in England, is there too.
55541.m: The Lake District is an area for walking.

55542.q: Which is the largest natural lake in England, in the Lake District?
55542.e: Windermere is the largest natural lake in England. It is over 15 kilometres long but only about 1.5 kilometres wide.
55542.m: Windermere is the largest lake in England.

55543.q: Which children's author lived in the Lake District and created Peter Rabbit?
55543.e: Beatrix Potter lived at Hill Top farm in the Lake District. She bought a lot of land and later gave it to nature conservation.
55543.m: Peter Rabbit was created by Beatrix Potter in the Lake District.

55544.q: What mainly shaped the valleys and lakes of the Lake District?
55544.e: In the Ice Age, glaciers carved out deep valleys. When the ice melted, they filled with water and became long lakes.
55544.m: Glaciers shaped the lakes of the Lake District.

55545.q: What has the Lake District been since 1951?
55545.e: The Lake District became a national park in 1951. Since 2017 it has also been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
55545.m: The Lake District is a national park.

55546.q: Where does the Lake District get its name from?
a: From a town by the sea
55546.e: The Lake District has many lakes, which were shaped by glaciers.
55546.m: The Lake District is named after its lakes.

55547.q: In which country is the famous stone circle Stonehenge?
55547.e: Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in the south of England. The huge stones were put up about 4500 years ago.

55548.q: How are the big lintel stones of Stonehenge placed?
55548.e: Two upright stones carry a lintel stone laid across the top. At Stonehenge these groups of three stones form a horseshoe.
55548.m: At Stonehenge, lintels lie on top of two upright stones.

55549.q: From which period does Stonehenge date?
55549.e: Stonehenge was built about 5000 to 4000 years ago in the New Stone Age. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.
55549.m: Stonehenge dates from the Stone Age.

55550.q: Which island in the Irish Sea belongs to the British Crown but is not part of the United Kingdom?
55550.e: The Isle of Man is a Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the Tynwald. It belongs neither to the United Kingdom nor to the EU.
55550.m: The Isle of Man is under the Crown but self-governing.

55551.q: In which building in London does the British Parliament meet?
55551.e: Parliament, with the House of Commons and the House of Lords, meets in the Palace of Westminster on the Thames. The palace was rebuilt after a fire in 1834.
55551.m: The British Parliament sits in the Palace of Westminster.

55552.q: In which church in London are British kings and queens crowned?
55552.e: Since 1066 almost all coronations have taken place in Westminster Abbey. Charles III was also crowned there in 2023.
55552.m: British monarchs are crowned in Westminster Abbey.

55553.q: Which event destroyed large parts of central London in 1666?
55553.e: The Great Fire of London raged for several days in 1666 and destroyed thousands of houses. Afterwards the city was rebuilt with stone houses.
55553.m: London burned in the Great Fire of 1666.

55554.q: What is the name of London's old city centre, which is now an important banking district?
55554.e: The City of London is the oldest part of the city and only about one square mile in size. Many banks and the Bank of England have their headquarters there.
55554.m: The City of London is London's financial centre.

55555.q: Which royal castle lies west of London right on the Thames?
55555.e: Windsor Castle stands on a hill above the Thames. It is said to be the oldest and largest lived-in castle in the world.
55555.m: Windsor Castle lies on the Thames.

55556.q: In which direction does the Thames flow from its source to its mouth?
55556.e: The Thames rises in the west of England and flows east through London. Its mouth is on the east coast.
55556.m: The Thames flows from west to east.

55557.q: Which title is traditionally held by the eldest son and heir of the British monarch?
55557.e: The heir to the throne usually receives the title Prince of Wales. Prince William has held it since 2022.
55557.m: The British heir to the throne is called the Prince of Wales.

55558.q: Where in Wales is there a village with one of the longest place names in Europe?
55558.e: The village of Llanfairpwllgwyngyll, whose full name is 58 letters long, is on Anglesey. In Welsh, the name describes where the church is.
55558.m: A village on Anglesey has a hugely long name.

55559.q: Which old language is spoken in Wales alongside English?
55559.e: Welsh is a Celtic language. In Wales, many signs are in English and Welsh.
55559.m: In Wales people also speak Welsh.

55561.q: Which range of hills is called the “backbone of England”?
55561.e: The Pennines run north to south from the Midlands almost to the Scottish border. That is why they are called the backbone of England.
55561.m: The Pennines are the backbone of England.

55562.q: Which prickly plant is a national symbol of Scotland?
55562.e: The thistle has been Scotland's emblem for centuries. A legend says it warned the Scots of a night attack.
55562.m: The thistle is Scotland's plant symbol.

55563.q: Why did many people have to leave the Scottish Highlands in the 18th and 19th centuries?
a: Landowners wanted room for sheep pastures
Everyone moved into the mountains willingly
55563.e: In the “Highland Clearances”, landowners drove out many small farmers so they could keep sheep. Many families emigrated to America or Australia.
55563.m: In the Highland Clearances, many people had to make way for sheep.

55564.q: Which item of clothing do men traditionally wear in the Scottish Highlands?
55564.e: The kilt is a checked wrap-around skirt made of wool. Its pattern, the tartan, often shows which clan someone belongs to.
55564.m: The kilt is the traditional garment of the Highlands.

55565.q: What does the Scottish word “glen” mean?
55565.e: In Scotland many valleys are called glens, for example Glen Nevis at the foot of Ben Nevis or Glen Coe.
55565.m: A glen is a valley in Scotland.

55566.q: In which year did most of Ireland become independent of the United Kingdom as the Irish Free State?
55566.e: The Irish Free State was created in 1922; the north-east of the island stayed with the United Kingdom. In 1949 the state became a republic.
55566.m: Most of Ireland has been independent since 1922.

55567.q: Roughly how high is the highest mountain in Ireland?
55567.e: The highest mountain in Ireland, Carrauntoohil, is about 1039 metres high. Ireland has no really high mountain ranges.
55567.m: Ireland's highest mountain is only about 1000 m high.

55568.q: In which year did Ireland join the European Community, today's EU?
55568.e: Ireland joined in 1973 together with the United Kingdom and Denmark. Membership brought the country a big economic boost.
55568.m: Ireland has been in the European Community since 1973.

55569.q: Which disaster from 1845 onwards led millions of people to leave Ireland?
55569.e: A plant disease destroyed the potato harvests, the most important food. About a million people died, and even more emigrated to America.
55569.m: Potato blight caused a great famine in Ireland.

55570.q: Roughly how many people live in the Republic of Ireland (as of 2025)?
55570.e: In 2025 about 5.5 million people lived in the Republic of Ireland. That is clearly fewer than in Switzerland with about 9 million.
55570.m: Ireland has clearly fewer inhabitants than Switzerland.

55571.q: What are the areas of Ireland called where Irish is still the everyday language?
55571.e: The Gaeltacht lies mainly on the west coast, for example in Donegal and Galway. There Irish is spoken in families and schools.
55571.m: In the Gaeltacht, Irish is spoken in everyday life.

55572.q: Which oldest university in Ireland stands in the centre of Dublin?
55572.e: Trinity College was founded in 1592. It is the oldest university in Ireland.
55572.m: Trinity College in Dublin is Ireland's oldest university.

55573.q: Where does the Ha'penny Bridge in Dublin get its name from?
55573.e: Anyone who wanted to cross the footbridge from 1816 had to pay half a penny. That is where the name Ha'penny Bridge comes from.
55573.m: Crossing the Ha'penny Bridge used to cost half a penny.

55574.q: How do trains travel between England and France across the English Channel today?
a: Through a tunnel under the sea
55574.e: The Channel Tunnel has linked England and France since 1994. It is about 50 kilometres long.
55574.m: A railway tunnel runs under the English Channel.

55575.q: Which largest island of England lies in the English Channel off Southampton?
55575.e: The Isle of Wight lies off the south coast of England. It is the largest island that belongs to England.
55575.m: The Isle of Wight is England's largest island.

55576.q: Which two countries does the Channel Tunnel link?
55576.e: The Channel Tunnel has linked England with France since 1994. Trains run directly from London to Paris.
55576.m: The Channel Tunnel links Great Britain with France.

55577.q: What travels through the Channel Tunnel?
55577.e: Only trains travel through the Channel Tunnel. Cars and lorries are loaded onto special car trains.
55577.m: Only trains travel through the Channel Tunnel.

55578.q: How was the Channel Tunnel built?
a: With boring machines from both sides
55578.e: Large tunnel boring machines dug towards each other from England and from France. They met under the sea in 1990.
55578.m: The Channel Tunnel was bored from both sides.

55579.q: Which record does the Channel Tunnel hold?
a: Longest undersea section of any railway tunnel
Longest road tunnel in the world
55579.e: About 38 kilometres of the Channel Tunnel lie under the sea. No other railway tunnel has such a long section under water.
55579.m: The Channel Tunnel has the longest undersea section in the world.

55580.q: Roughly how long does the car train journey through the Channel Tunnel take?
55580.e: The shuttle train takes about 35 minutes from terminal to terminal. The crossing by ferry takes much longer.
55580.m: You travel through the Channel Tunnel in about half an hour.

55581.q: What does the English word “henge” mean for structures like Stonehenge?
a: A round area with a ditch and bank
A stone wall around a village
55581.e: A henge is a circular site from the New Stone Age, surrounded by an earth bank and a ditch. Stonehenge has such a circular ditch.
55581.m: A henge is a round area with a bank and a ditch.

55582.q: What type of rock are the big sarsen stones of Stonehenge made of?
55582.e: The big stones are sarsens, a very hard sandstone. They come from the area around Marlborough, about 25 kilometres to the north.
55582.m: The big stones of Stonehenge are made of hard sandstone.

55583.q: Like Stonehenge, Avebury in England is known for something from the Stone Age. What?
55583.e: Avebury has the largest stone circle in Europe. It even surrounds parts of the village and, like Stonehenge, is a World Heritage Site.
55583.m: Europe's largest stone circle is at Avebury.

55584.q: In which French region does the Seine rise?
55584.e: The Seine rises on the Langres Plateau in Burgundy. From there it flows north-west through Paris to the sea.
55584.m: The source of the Seine is in Burgundy.

55585.q: Near which port does the Seine flow into the sea?
55585.e: The Seine flows into the sea through a wide estuary near Le Havre and Honfleur. Le Havre is one of the most important ports in France.
55585.m: The Seine reaches the sea at Le Havre.

55586.q: Which city does the Seine flow through?
55586.e: The Seine flows right through Paris. Just before the city, the Marne, its longest tributary, joins it.

55588.q: Which famous cathedral stands on the Île de la Cité, an island in the Seine?
55588.e: Notre-Dame Cathedral stands on the Île de la Cité in the middle of Paris. After the fire of 2019 it reopened in 2024.
55588.m: Notre-Dame stands on an island in the Seine.

55589.q: On which hill in the north of Paris does the Sacré-Cœur Basilica stand?
55589.e: The white Sacré-Cœur Basilica stands on Montmartre, the highest hill in Paris. The area used to be a well-known meeting place for painters.
55589.m: Sacré-Cœur sits on top of Montmartre.

55590.q: Which monument stands at the top end of the Avenue des Champs-Élysées?
55590.e: The Arc de Triomphe stands on the Place Charles-de-Gaulle at the top end of the Champs-Élysées. Napoleon had it built from 1806.
55590.m: The Arc de Triomphe crowns the Champs-Élysées.

55591.q: Which is the longest river in France?
55591.e: The Loire is about 1000 kilometres long and flows only through France. It rises in the Massif Central.
55591.m: The Loire is the longest river in France.

55592.q: Roughly how long is the Loire?
55592.e: The Loire is about 1000 kilometres long. It flows entirely through France.
55592.m: The Loire is roughly a thousand kilometres long.

55593.q: Into which sea does the Loire flow?
55593.e: The Loire flows west and reaches the Atlantic at Saint-Nazaire.
55593.m: The Loire flows into the Atlantic.

55594.q: Which of these cities lies on the Loire?
55594.e: Tours lies in the middle of the Loire Valley. Lyon is on the Rhône and Saône, Rouen on the Seine and Toulouse on the Garonne.
55594.m: Tours is a city on the Loire.

55595.q: What is the Loire Valley especially famous for?
55595.e: In the Loire Valley, kings and nobles built magnificent châteaux such as Chambord. That is why it is also called the “Valley of the Kings”.
55595.m: The Loire Valley is known for its châteaux.

55596.q: What grows in large amounts on the slopes of the Loire Valley?
55596.e: The mild climate of the Loire Valley is well suited to growing wine. Vegetables and fruit also grow well there.
55596.m: A lot of wine is grown in the Loire Valley.

55597.q: In which mountains does the Loire rise?
55597.e: The Loire and its tributary the Allier come from the Massif Central, an old volcanic range in the middle of France.
55597.m: The Loire rises in the Massif Central.

55598.q: In which country does the Garonne rise?
55598.e: The Garonne rises in the Val d'Aran in the Spanish Pyrenees. Only after that does it flow into France.
55598.m: The Garonne has its source in Spain.

55599.q: Which city on the Garonne is called the “Ville rose” because of its brick buildings?
55599.e: Toulouse is known for its reddish brick buildings. That is why it is called “the pink city” in French.
55599.m: Toulouse is the pink city on the Garonne.

55600.q: Which port city on the Garonne is world-famous for its wine?
55600.e: Bordeaux lies on the Garonne and is the centre of one of the best-known wine regions in the world. Its old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
55600.m: Bordeaux is a wine city on the Garonne.

55601.q: What is the name of the estuary that the Garonne and Dordogne form together?
55601.e: North of Bordeaux the Garonne and the Dordogne meet. Together they form the Gironde, one of the largest estuaries in Europe.
55601.m: The Garonne and Dordogne together form the Gironde.

55602.q: Which canal links the Garonne at Toulouse with the Mediterranean?
55602.e: The Canal du Midi was built in the 17th century and runs from Toulouse to the Mediterranean. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
55602.m: The Canal du Midi links Toulouse with the Mediterranean.

55603.q: Which industry is especially important in Toulouse on the Garonne?
55603.e: Many aircraft are built and satellites developed in Toulouse. The city is a European centre of the aerospace industry.
55603.m: Toulouse is a city of aircraft and satellites.

55604.q: What is the mascaret on the Garonne?
a: A tidal wave that travels upstream
55604.e: At a strong high tide the sea pushes water into the Gironde and creates a wave that travels upstream. Some surfers ride it.
55604.m: The mascaret is a tidal wave that travels upstream.

55605.q: In which country is the Massif Central?
55605.e: The Massif Central is an upland area in the south of France. Its highest peak, the Puy de Sancy, is about 1886 metres high.
55605.m: The Massif Central is in France.

55606.q: What are the many round mountains of the Chaîne des Puys in the Massif Central?
55606.e: The Chaîne des Puys is made up of about 80 extinct volcanoes. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018.
55606.m: The Chaîne des Puys is a chain of extinct volcanoes.

55607.q: Which region in the Massif Central is known for its old volcanoes?
55607.e: There are many extinct volcanoes in the Auvergne, for example the Puy de Dôme near Clermont-Ferrand.
55607.m: The Auvergne is France's volcano country.

55608.q: What is the Millau Viaduct in France famous for?
a: It is one of the highest bridges in the world
It is the longest tunnel in the world
It is the oldest Roman bridge
